instructions:
You are the resilience analyst of an AI-driven chaos-engineering agent. The system under test is Google's Online
Boutique (11 gRPC microservices) on single-node Kubernetes. You get the measured facts of every experiment, the
dependency map, the baseline, the planner's predictions and how they held, anchor scores computed by code, and the
catalog of fixes.

Produce:
1. Findings = weaknesses, ranked by severity (most severe first). Severity scale: {"critical": "users cannot shop or check out (outage or most requests failing) and nothing contains it", "high": "a core flow (product, cart, checkout) breaks or becomes unusably slow (seconds), or recovery is slow", "medium": "noticeable degradation with a workaround or limited scope (one flow, moderate slowdown)", "low": "minor impact, or a configuration weakness without measured user impact yet"}.
   Each finding: affected services, the run ids that show it (exactly as given), the measured numbers, the root
   cause (explain the mechanism, e.g. sequential calls without deadlines amplify latency), ONE fix from the fix
   catalog with concrete parameters, why it addresses the root cause, the improvement you expect, and the
   experiment to re-run after the fix (same type/target/params as the evidence run when possible).
   Positive findings (e.g. graceful degradation) may be included as low severity with a code_change or posture fix
   only if useful; do not invent problems without evidence. Merge findings that share one root cause.
2. Resilience scores: for EVERY service in the anchors table, score each rubric dimension 0-100:
   {"availability": "Did users keep getting successful responses? 100 = no extra errors; 70 = a few % errors or short error bursts; 40 = sustained errors on some flows; 0 = most requests failed.", "latency": "How much slower did user flows get (worst p95 vs baseline)? 100 = < 1.5x; 80 = ~3x; 60 = ~10x; 30 = ~50x; 0 = several seconds / timeouts.", "recovery": "How fast were users back to normal after the fault ended? 100 = immediately or never impacted; 75 = ~30 s; 50 = ~60 s; 0 = not recovered within 180 s.", "containment": "Did the failure stay contained? 100 = callers degraded gracefully, no spread; lower when flows that depend on the service broke, when unrelated flows/pods were hit, or when the guard had to stop the experiment.", "posture": "Static resilience configuration: 100 = >= 2 replicas, readiness + liveness probes, CPU/memory limits; single replica -40, missing readiness -20, missing liveness -10, missing limits -20."}
   Start from the anchor and stay within +-15 of it; deviate only with a reason (e.g. impact
   on an optional feature like ads matters less; a slow recovery on the checkout path matters more). Untested
   services: score availability/latency/recovery/containment from posture and dependencies, close to the anchor
   (anchors for untested dimensions are null - use your judgement and say so). Choose a criticality weight per
   service (0.5-3) reflecting business impact (checkout path and entrypoint high, ads/recommendations low).
3. Explain how you weighed services, review how well the planner's predictions held, and list limitations
   (single VM, small probe, short experiments).
Use only facts you are given or fetch with the tools. Answer only with the structured report.

output.summary: The most serious measured weakness is shippingservice unavailability: checkout failed on every sampled request, home latency rose sharply, and the run was stopped by the error-rate guard. Separate tests showed checkout latency increasing about 3–4× under paymentservice network loss and checkoutservice CPU saturation, without errors. Paymentservice memory-stress tests did not cause OOMs or errors, though checkout latency also rose during those runs. Eight of the eleven application services were not directly tested, so their scores are cautious estimates based on configuration and dependency reach.

findings.title: Shippingservice failure breaks checkout and produces severe latency spillover
findings.evidence: The run was aborted after 2.6 s of fault when the error-rate guard measured 24% errors (impact error rate 25%). Checkout had 100% errors across 4 requests. Home p95 was 512.0 ms versus a 17.1 ms baseline (29.94×); overall peak p95 was 779.3 ms. The guard stopped the run, and the timeline returned to OK by 9.6 s after injection.
findings.root_cause: shippingservice is a single replica on the checkout path and is also called by frontend. When it is unavailable, the dependency failure is not contained: checkout fails and even home requests experience a large latency increase. The guard limited the duration of the outage, but did not prevent the user impact.
findings.fix_rationale: A second stateless shippingservice replica reduces the single-pod failure risk and provides another serving instance if one pod becomes unavailable.
findings.expected_improvement: On rerun, a single shippingservice pod failure should no longer make checkout uniformly fail; checkout errors and the home-flow latency spike should be substantially reduced. The experiment may still expose limits from running both replicas on one node.

findings.title: Paymentservice faults propagate as checkout latency
findings.evidence: Checkout p95 was 40.2 ms (1.86× its 21.6 ms baseline) during 124 MB memory stress, 63.9 ms (2.96×) during 128 MB stress, and 83.1 ms (3.85×) during 5% uncorrelated packet loss. All three runs had 0% errors and no paymentservice restarts. In the 128 MB run, paymentservice memory peaked at 67.3 MiB against a 128 MiB limit.
findings.root_cause: Paymentservice is a direct checkout dependency, and the measured delay under stress and packet loss is visible in the checkout flow. The experiments do not establish the exact RPC retry or deadline behavior, but they show that paymentservice-related delay is not fully isolated from checkout latency.

fix.change: Set a 300 ms end-to-end gRPC deadline for checkoutservice calls to paymentservice; ensure any retry shares the remaining deadline and is capped at one attempt.

findings.fix_rationale: A bounded RPC budget prevents slow payment calls and retries from extending checkout latency without limit during worse transport or service faults. This is an advisory code change and should be checked for its error-versus-latency tradeoff.
findings.expected_improvement: The rerun should keep the same fault from causing unbounded checkout waits and should preserve the observed zero-error behavior if calls complete within the deadline. Confirm both checkout p95 and error rate, since a deadline can turn slow responses into explicit failures.

findings.title: Checkoutservice CPU limit is fully saturated under CPU stress
findings.evidence: Checkout p95 was 70.6 ms versus a 21.6 ms baseline (3.27×), with 0% errors. checkoutservice reached 100.2% of its 200m CPU limit and 100% peak CPU throttling. The other measured flows had no errors.
findings.root_cause: The single checkoutservice pod is constrained by a 200m CPU limit. Under the tested CPU stress, it reached that limit and was fully throttled, increasing latency on the checkout path.
findings.fix_rationale: Increasing the CPU limit gives checkoutservice more headroom and directly addresses the measured CPU saturation and throttling; memory remains at its existing limit because this run did not indicate memory pressure.
findings.expected_improvement: With the same stress, checkoutservice should spend less time throttled and checkout p95 should move closer to baseline, while errors remain absent.

output.score_explanation: For directly tested services, scores stay within 15 points of their supplied anchors and reflect measured flow impact as well as service-level outcomes. Shippingservice scores emphasize the checkout failure and home-flow latency spillover, while its recovery score reflects the timeline returning to OK by 9.6 seconds. Paymentservice retained full availability and recovery scores because its tests produced no errors or restarts, but latency and containment reflect the checkout slowdown. For the eight untested services, availability, latency, recovery and containment are estimates near the posture anchor, adjusted modestly for replica count, statefulness and dependency reach; posture is 60 throughout because the map shows one replica, both probes and resource limits. Criticality weights are capped at 3.0 and prioritize the frontend, cart path and checkout dependencies over ads and recommendations.
output.planner_review: Predictions were directionally useful on the shippingservice outage, correctly anticipating severe impact and an abort, but the predicted affected flows (checkout and view_cart) differed from observed checkout and home; view_cart had no sampled requests. The 124 MB paymentservice memory-stress prediction was refuted: there were no checkout errors or abort, and memory peaked at 33.7 MiB. The subsequent 128 MB run prediction was confirmed for no errors and completion, with moderate slowdown. The paymentservice network-loss prediction matched the affected checkout flow, no-error outcome and completion, but overpredicted the slowdown severity band. The checkoutservice CPU-stress prediction matched the moderate slowdown and completion but labeled checkout as an affected flow when the run summary did not; per-flow measurements nevertheless show checkout p95 at 3.27× baseline. Overall, predictions captured broad outcomes better than precise flow attribution or severity.
limitations: The system runs on a single Kubernetes node, so adding replicas does not provide node-level fault tolerance and may introduce resource contention.
The probe is small: most completed runs had only 11–24 requests per flow, and the aborted shippingservice run had only four checkout requests.
The shippingservice fault was active for only 2.6 seconds before the guard aborted it, limiting conclusions about a sustained outage.
Only five experiments were run, covering CPU stress, memory stress, network loss and pod failure; other services and fault types remain untested.
There are no internal call traces here to confirm the exact RPC timing, retry or deadline behavior behind the observed latency propagation.
Scores for services without direct experiments are estimates from the dependency map and static posture, not measured resilience.
